comparisons.peer_summary: On December 20, 2024, the CFPB filed a lawsuit against BANA and co-defendants in the U.S. District Court for the District of Arizona, alleging violations of the Consumer Financial Protection Act and the Electronic Fund Transfer Act related to fraud protection and investigation of disputed Zelle transfers.

Similarly, BAC is facing a lawsuit from the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) regarding its processing of Zelle network payments and alleged failures to protect consumers from fraud under the Electronic Fund Transfer Act and Consumer Financial Protection Act.

On December 20, 2024, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) filed suit against BANA, JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A., Wells Fargo Bank, N.A., and Early Warning Services, LLC in the U.S. District Court for the District of Arizona with respect to BANA's and co-defendants' processing of electronic payments of funds through the Zelle network.

The CFPB alleges that BANA and its co-defendants violated the Consumer Financial Protection Act by not adequately protecting consumers from fraud on the Zelle network and the Electronic Fund Transfer Act by not reasonably investigating and reimbursing disputed Zelle transfers, and seeks both monetary and injunctive relief.

comparisons.peer_topic: Intercompany lending restrictions and capital limits
comparisons.peer_summary: U.S. federal law restricts JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. and subsidiaries from lending to the Parent Company or affiliates unless secured, with covered transactions limited to 10% of a subsidiary's capital individually and 20% in aggregate.
comparisons.comparison: Both disclosures address legal and regulatory restrictions governing the relationship between the parent company and its bank subsidiaries. MS's disclosure involves regulatory inquiries into the structure and compliance of its 'affiliate bank deposit program,' implying scrutiny of inter-affiliate flows and activities. JPM explicitly details the U.S. federal law restrictions prohibiting its bank subsidiary from lending to the Parent Company or affiliates unless secured, limiting such 'covered transactions' to specific capital percentages. Both highlight the regulatory boundary between the banking entity and the holding company/affiliates.

Restrictions imposed by U.S. federal law prohibit JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A., and its subsidiaries, from lending to JPMorgan Chase & Co. ("Parent Company") and certain of its affiliates unless the loans are secured in specified amounts.

In addition, unless collateralized with cash or US Government debt obligations, covered transactions are generally limited to 10% of the banking subsidiary's total capital, as determined by the risk-based capital guidelines; the aggregate amount of covered transactions between any banking subsidiary and all of its affiliates is limited to 20% of the banking subsidiary's total capital.
